speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: COMMISSIONS AND OTHER COSTS
subsubtopic: CASH AND CON- VERSION SUBSCRIPTIONS-APPRECIATION OF SERVICES OF COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I think I should make a statement regarding the second victory loan before the house adjourns. The main part of this statement will relate to commissions and other remuneration paid in connection with the sale of the second victory loan bonds. I make this statement because certain hon. members of the house have been good enough to call to my attention certain reports which are apparently circulating in some sections of the country. These are so obviously false as to suggest that they have been inspired by sources which have a selfish interest in undermining and impeding Canada's war effort.
Unfortunately it will be some time yet before all the payments have been made and the returns completed in connection with the loan, and therefore I cannot now give the actual dollar amounts of payments that will be made to those who rendered services in connection with the campaign. However, I can and wish to give the house the basis upon which the payments will be made.
First, let me deal with the commissions paid to individual salesmen. The basis of these commissions will be five-eighths of one per cent on subscriptions to the twelve-year
bonds and three-eighths of one per cent on the six-year bonds. This represents an increase of one-eighth of one per cent compared with what was paid in connection with 1941 victory loan, but it must be noted that this time no commission will be paid on subscriptions classified as employee subscriptions. Moreover, no commission will be paid on conversion subscriptions to the two and one-half year bonds which were not issued for cash, or on subscriptions from subscribers included in the special names category. Last year we found that fin a good many instances, particularly in the case of salesmen working in rural districts or other districts which for one reason or another did not represent good sales territory, the amount of commissions paid served to do little more than cover out-ofpocket expenses of the salesmen. Provision was therefore made this time for more extensive pooling of part of the commission by provincial and local committees so that fair treatment could be rendered to each salesman no matter what the type of sales territory in which he was assigned to work. My hope is that this arrangement will result in reasonably fair treatment to all the individual salesmen. In this connection it should be remembered that the salesmen used in the campaign were drawn away from their usual occupations, and had not only to devote their full time to the sales of bonds while the campaign was on but also had to spend considerable time in preparation and training during the three weeks period before the campaign actually commenced.
Next I deal with the remuneration to banks, trust and loan companies, Quebec savings banks and other savings institutions (province of Ontario savings offices, Alberta treasury branches, and La Federation des Caisses Populates Desjardins). No selling commission of any kind will be paid on sales made to the public by the various branches of the banks or these other financial institutions. However, we will pay a service fee for the varied services they rendered in entering subscriptions and handling the payment and delivery of the bonds to purchasers. This service fee will be at a rate of one-quarter of one per cent of the par value of bonds serviced by each such institution calculated in accordance with the regulations.
With regard to the remuneration to be paid to investment dealers and stockbrokers, provision has been made for investigation of the services rendered and recommendation to me of a fair basis of remuneration for such services by a committee consisting of the chairman of the national war finance committee, the securities advisor of the Bank of Canada, and the deputy minister of finance. In arriv-
Second Victory Loan

mg at this basis of remuneration, the committee will take into account the number of different types of personnel made available to the national war finance committee for varying terms of employment, -which extended over a period of four months in many cases, and will also have reasonable regard to the past record of performance of the various firms in connection with dominion loan campaigns.
The house may recall that the total expenses in connection with the first victory loan campaign, including not only commissions and other remuneration for services rendered but also advertising and publicity expenses, printing and distribution of bonds, et cetera, amounted to only 1-09 per cent of the total amount of the issue. It is anticipated that total expenditures in connection with the second victory loan campaign will represent a slightly lower percentage of the total issue. There has been some criticism in certain quarters of some aspects of the loan campaign. In my opinion these criticisms are unfounded. The campaign itself was a striking success, the reports I have received pay uniform tribute to the highly efficient organization which was developed, and I think the house will agree that the percentage cost figures which I have just indicated represent a very economical cost of raising a public loan of this magnitude and character.
In conclusion, I wish to express at this time and in this place not only the keen appreciation of the government and myself, out also I hope of this parliament, for the one services rendered in this very important campaign not only by members of the national war finance committee, which includes the provincial chairmen, but also by a great many other voluntary workers in provincial and local committees who gave unsparingly of their time and energy to make the campaign the success it proved- to be. Because, apparently, there has been a rumour circulating to the contrary, I wish to emphasize the fact that with the single exception of one provincial chairman serving in a western province and who because he is devoting his full time to the work of the national war finance committee receives a modest compensation, these persons gave their services without any remuneration.
Before I take my seat, it may be of interest to the house if I now give the latest figures we / have available in regard to the results of the loan. Figures compiled as at March 14th, show a total number of subscribers of 1,643,013, and- a total volume of subscriptions of 1993,884,350. Of the latter total, $841,766,350 represented cash subscrip-

tions, and the remainder, $152,118,000, represented conversion subscriptions. These figures are not as yet final but they will probably approximate the final results. The house, I think, will agree that these are astounding results for a loan offered to the public in the middle of winter and only one month prior to the due date of heavily increased income tax payments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one of the members who asked that the committee on agriculture should be called together to consider the bills relating to agriculture, I should like to make a few observations on this matter.
Last year I was a member of the committee which dealt with pensions and returned soldier problems. That committee accomplished a good deal of excellent work. We met as a group of returned men, not as members of political parties, to consider the recommendations which had been made, and as a result of our work w*e offered certain suggestions to the government, which to a great extent were accepted. I was in hopes that when the agriculture committee met, the procedure would be something similar, that we would meet as a group of members representing agricultural constituencies, to consider the problems of the wheat growers of western Canada.
I am sorry to say that this was not the case. Even before the committee met, its work was prejudiced by the remarks of certain members on the government side of the house. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross), speaking the day before the bill was referred to the committee, is reported at page 1382 of Hansard to have said:
The changes in policy this year, as brought down by the government, have been accepted by hon. members in the government and followers of the government in the house, and for that reason they will finally pass the house as they are. No number of speeches made by hon. members can change that position. They did not even know what was going to happen until it came down in the house.

Wheat Board Act
That is an entirely wrong spirit in which to refer any measure to a committee. We found when the committee met that the same condition prevailed in the committee. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) told us that we could make representations, but that it was altogether unlikely that the government would be prepared to accept them, and that it had already viewed these bills from [DOT]every angle. He pointed out that everything that could be said with respect to them had already been said in the cabinet, and it was doubtful whether anything we would recommend would be accepted, if it entailed any further expenditure of money.
Under such circumstances it was pretty hard in committee to get anything which would give western agriculture a better deal than it had been receiving in the past. We did, however, recommend certain changes. We recommended a change with respect to basic acreage, as covered in section 3 of Bill No. 12. But that recommendation was not accepted by the government, and the bill went through in almost the same form as that in which it had been presented to the committee.
There were many of us who thought that in the consideration of Bill No. 14, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, a change should have been made to bring into the bill the principle of insurance. We were told that this was ultra vires of the British North America Act. It will be remembered, however, that when the government wished to introduce unemployment insurance it found a means to get round that difficulty; and I am sure, if it desired, it could find the means of developing from the Prairie Farm Assistance Act a comprehensive insurance scheme. A recommendation which was made in the committee that the government give further study to this matter was voted down. The fact that the committee on agriculture voted down a recommendation that the government should consider and study the matter of crop insurance does not seem to reflect the exercise of any great amount of intelligence. In the United States this matter has been considered for a number of years, and they have introduced a comprehensive scheme of crop insurance not only for wheat but for cotton and many other agricultural products.
These three bills taken together do not place the western wheat growers in any better position to-day than that which they occupied last year. Last year, under the prairie farm income legislation the farmers of western Canada were paid approximately $20,000,000. Under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, as it operated last year, they were paid something over $11,000,000. This year that act has been amended so as to exclude
those having crops of from eight to twelve bushels to the acre. Last year $7,000,000 of the money paid under the act was paid to this class. Wheat acreage reduction payments last year were made on the basis of $4 an acre; this year the basis is reduced to $2 an acre. This means that $11,000,000 less will be paid under the act next year.
The basic acreage under the wheat acreage reduction bill was changed. Under the new regulations it will mean that the bonus will be paid on a million less acres than last year. This means another $2,000,000 less that the farmers of western Canada will receive. In all, a total of $40,000,000 less will be paid under the regulations this year than was paid last year. If we take the crop we had last year, one of 200,000,000 bushels, and pay an additional 20 cents a bushel on it, as is recommended under this measure, we find that we have an additional payment of $40,000,000. On the other hand-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member is discussing this bill at all. He is discussing other measures which were before the house on earlier occasions. This bill provides only two things: first, to change the price from 70 cents to 90 cents and, second, to include the word "mills". My hon. friend is discussing the acreage bonus, and matters of that kind, which have nothing to do with the bill.
Mr. MaeINNIS: On the point of order, while I did not take part in the discussion, my understanding is that all the bills were discussed interchangeably, or at the same time. I believe that was done to facilitate discussion on the whole question. If the hon. member for Melfort believes that that procedure is necessary on this occasion, I suggest he should be allowed to proceed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I would draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that an arrangement was reached in preliminary discussions, on second reading of these bills in the house. The bills were then sent to committee, and this bill was reported back without amendment. I suggest it is stretching the understanding too far if we are to permit the same discussion at this stage.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I was discussing the other bills only as they relate to this one. I have, however, completed that phase of the matter, and I shall not pursue it further.
With respect to the bill before the committee, we were informed in the committee on agriculture that we could not be told the price we were receiving for our wheat
Wheat Board Act

because the British government did not think it advisable to state the price at this time. But it will be noticed that the British government have allowed proper prices on other agricultural products. We know the price for cheese, and the prices for pork, bacon and other products have been made public. But there seems to be some deep dark secret so far as wheat is concerned. Perhaps there is a good reason for this secrecy, but I have never been able to see what it was. It seemed very unfair to me that the British government should be willing to pay their own farmers the cost of production, but that it should insist that the price paid to the farmers of western Canada should be less than the cost of production. That does not develop good-will or unity among British countries, but it is a condition which has prevailed up to this year.
Under the billion dollar gift to Britain that condition has been changed entirely. The matter is now in the hands of the Canadian government, and it seems most unfair to us in western Canada to know that our wheat is being sold to Great Britain below the cost of production, thereby compelling us to pay an unfair share of that billion dollar gift. Everything else going to Great Britain under that gift is being sent at a price which at least equals the cost of production. We in western Canada feel that our contribution to the gift should be at a rate equal to our cost.
There are three things these bills do not do which I believe they should do. It seems to me that the 8 to 12 bushel class should not have been eliminated from the provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and there should have been no change in the basic acreage provision in the wheat acreage reduction bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) was quite in order when he contended that hon. members should keep within the limits of the bill. Later on there will be another bill having to do with wheat acreage, but at the present time we are dealing only with the wheat bonus.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
As I say, the rate should not have been cut. This amendment to the wheat board act provides for a . price this year of 90 cents a bushel, but I believe that this price should have been at least $1 a bushel, Fort William, plus participation certificates which would bring the farmer at least a parity price for his product. It seems to me that with these bills we are doing just what the hon. member for St. Antoine-

Westmount (Mr. Abbott) referred to about a year ago when he stated that some people believed they were thinking, when they were in reality only rearranging their prejudices. It seems to me that in these bills we are simply rearranging the payments to the farmers of western Canada. We are paying but little more than was paid last year, and with the wheat grower working under the conditions which prevail to-day, this seems to me to be most unfair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: It has been said that this 90 cents is below the cost of production. I can visualize a man with a five-bushel crop and another one with a twenty-bushel crop, and I cannot just understand what amount a farmer would have to get to cover his cost of production. Could the hon. member tell me what the cost of production really is on a bushel of wheat?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: The cost of production must always be figured on an average yield. The average yield in western Canada for many years has been between 16 and 18 bushels per acre. In my own section of the country our crops are larger than that. My own average for the past twenty years has been over 30 bushels per acre, but I grow wheat only on land that is specially prepared. You must take the average in arriving at these figures.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: In other words, this 90-cent price would amply pay some farmers, while it would not pay others; would that be correct?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
There would be few
farmers in western Canada who would have made a profit at 90 cents, taking the average for the past ten or twenty years. There may be exceptional cases where a profit would be made, but they would be exceptional. Western Canada asked for a parity price taking 1926-29 as a base, which would be much easier to arrive at than the cost of production. I have in my hand an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 4, dealing with what the western farmer is receiving to-day for his wheat. This reads:
The prairie wheat producers' purchasing power dropped to its lowest point in ten years in 1941, down nearly 21 points from 1940, an index prepared by dominion bureau of statistics showed to-day.
The index was based entirely on wheat. In cases where wheat farmers have turned to production of coarse grains or other products, their 1941 purchasing power compared favourably with that of 1940, officials said.
With yield per acre, farm price per bushel and value per acre taken into account, the bureau index for 1941 stood at 33-3 against 54-2 in 1940, 63-8 in 1939, 44-7 in 1935, 89-3 in 1928 and 100-1 in 1927.

Wheat Board Act
The index basis of 100 established in 1913, when yield per acre was 20'8 bushels, farm price 65 cents a bushel and value per acre was $13.62. In 1941 the yield per acre was 12-9 bushels, farm price 49 cents and value per acre $6.38.
The bureau noted the 1941 average yield was the lowest since 1927. In the present crop year, the farm price of wheat averaged 49-2 cents a bushel from August to December, or 2'4 cents a bushel less than the 1940-41 crop year average. The average value per acre of $6.38 in 1941 was the lowest reported since 1933.
I contend that the western farmer is entitled to at least a parity price for his wheat. That is what the delegation which came to Ottawa asked for; that is all western agriculture has ever asked for-equal treatment with other groups in the dominion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, what I shall have to say has been said year after year and I expect it to receive the same consideration now that it has received in the past. When this delegation of 400 from Saskatchewan, accompanied by representatives from Manitoba and Alberta, came down here, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) agreed that their demands were reasonable and fair. On one occasion the Prime Minister went so far as to say that the wheat situation was Canada's problem. I wonder what the Prime Minister is doing about it? Is he going to make it the farmers' problem or Canada's problem as a whole? We have not received the same consideration as that which has been accorded to other groups. We have been picked out and treated as a poor relation. As has been pointed out by the previous speaker, we have been no better off this last year than we were before. I think this fact must be recognized, regardless of any figures which may be placed before the committee. We know from experience that we are in no better position to-day than we were in the past.
We are asking for parity prices for agricultural products, not for one or two products but for all. This group with which I am associated and for which I am now speaking have suggested for a number of years that a price of 95 cents per bushel at the local elevator should be paid. The cost of production has increased tremendously because of the war, and this year we asked for at least $1 per bushel at the local elevators. Of course this would apply only where a farmer has a crop. Where he has no crop, some sound system of crop insurance should be put into effect. This could be done quite easily by amending the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Consideration of this matter was refused by the agriculture committee, for what reason I do not know. Perhaps the
main reason was prejudice and ignorance of the question under discussion. Any one who uses his brains for the purpose for which they were given would not refuse to ask the government to investigate the feasibility of instituting a sound policy of crop insurance.
I think it is admitted that we are not being treated the same as other citizens of Canada. Speaking on March 10, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) had this to say, as reported on page 1211 of Hansard:
I would say to him that any member of this house who carries back into western Canada the government's policy in relation to wheat and its policy in relation to other farm products can stand before any audience and explain to the people there that this is the best that can be done under the conditions with which we are confronted in the Dominion of Canada to-day, and the best that has been done in an attempt to settle their problems at any time.
Two wrongs, Mr. Chairman, never did make a right. I say without fear of contradiction that the wheat growers of western Canada have not received the cost of production since 1929, thirteen years ago. Put any other class in Canada in that position-industrialists, bankers, insurance men, or any other group-and after they have been producing below the cost of production for thirteen years what would you have? You would have sit-down strikes all over the country. But the farmers have never gone on a sit-down strike, and so I say that they are among the most loyal citizens of this country. We have also done our share in sending fighting men to the front, and the Minister of Finance will bear me out when I say that the farmers have done more than they were really able to in subscribing such large amounts to the victory loan, about which the minister spoke a few moments ago.
The Minister of Agriculture went on to say in that same speech:
We are taking every last dollar out of the treasury of Canada to deal with these problems which we feel it is safe to take at this present time.
Every other class is accorded its full share before the farmers are even considered. Why should we be treated as the orphans of this country? Why do we have to take the treatment of a stepmother, and carry on below the cost of production? I can see no reason for it. When money is required to pay interest on our national debt or to provide supplies for our fighting forces we can always float a loan -and just here let me say that the Minister of Finance has neglected the one institution which should do the most of Canada's financing outside of the money that is raised by taxation, and that is the Bank of Canada. The Minister of Finance seems to have neglected it entirely. Apparently his advisers and the rulers of this
Wheat Board Act

country have seen fit to decree that the farmers must continue in their present condition of poverty.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Yes, because for a number of
years past we have produced figures in this house, supported by argument, to show that the farmers have been and are still producing at below the cost of production, yet the government has not seen fit to alter that condition. As I see it, we shall have to have others on the treasury benches before the farmers will get fair treatment. It is my intention when I go back to my constituency to tell the farmers, as I shall continue to tell this house, that until they organize and vote in their own interest when election day comes, they can expect no better treatment than they are receiving and have been receiving for years past.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture a question based on the quotation from one of his addresses in this house which the hon. member for Battle River has just made, to the effect that the government was taking out of the treasury to deal with agricultural problems every last dollar it felt safe in taking. If funds were made available to the department for raising the price of wheat from 70 cents to $1 or to a parity price or whatever is considered a just price, would the minister go so far as to recommend to his department that this money actually be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: In the first place, Mr. Chairman, I made my speech on the second reading of the bill, and the statement which has just been quoted is fully explained in that speech. If my hon. friend wishes to read it he will find the explanation there. In the second place, this bill is introduced not by me 'but by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. No amount of money will be paid into my department, or for that matter into the Department of Trade and Commerce, to be paid out on wheat.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Then I will ask my question of whichever minister is responsible. It is a pertinent question, and if the Minister of Trade and Commerce is the responsible minister I should like to hear his reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: No money is paid into a department to be paid out on wheat. The wheat is delivered at the elevators in western Canada, and the amount paid out on the wheat is paid out through those elevators. There is no money paid out on wheat through any department of the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I think the ministry understand the question which I am trying to have

answered, and it is a fundamental point. The government has taken the position, as one would assume from the quotation from the speech of the Minister of Agriculture, that the reason the farmers are not paid more for their wheat is that there are not sufficient funds in the treasury. Is that so or is it not? I ask this further question: If the funds were made available for that purpose, would the government go so far as to recommend a price of SI or SL40 or whatever the parity price may be?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Parliament has to make the funds available.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: What has the Minister of Trade and Commerce to say?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: The question is based on a statement alleged to have been made by my colleague -the Minister of Agriculture, not on a statement made by me, and I do not think the question can properly be addressed to me. In any event it is more or less a catch-question; I do not think the hon. member is really serious in expecting an answer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: It is right enough that the Minister of Trade and Commerce should -not be held to account for the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I am much in earnest in asking the question and in expecting an answer. It has been definitely established, I -think, by all those who have spoken on hehalf of the agriculturists that they are deserving of far more consideration than they have received as compared with other classes in Canada. My opinion is that the reason the farmer is not being helped more is that the government is limited in its assistance to the farmers because of its financial policy and nothing else. If that is not correct I should like to be told so.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: That is not correct.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Then I cannot understand the statement of the Minister of Agriculture that the government is taking every dollar out of the treasury to help the farmers which it feels safe in taking. Certainly more funds can be made available, and if more funds can be made available I see absolutely no reason why the farmers should not receive $1 or $1.40 for their wheat.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I had not intended to take part in this discussion, but the point raised by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl) is an interesting one and, I think, should be answered. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) will

War Risk Insurance
not answer it I suppose we shall have to wait until the appropriation bill is before us and get the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to answer it. All the farmers' organizations requested a price of $1 a bushel, and I do not think the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Agriculture or any other minister has endeavoured to show that $1 a bushel would be an unfair price. The Minister of Agriculture, on the contrary, has stressed the fact that the government is paying every last cent out of the treasury to help the farmers, that it is scraping the bottom, so to speak. If SI a bushel is a fair price, and if the government feels that to pay the farmer more than ninety cents a bushel would, by increasing the effective demand of the farmers, be likely to bring about inflation, could the government not make up the difference between ninety cents and SI a bushel by giving the farmers war savings certificates maturing, we will say, at the end of the war? Then, as they would not be able to cash them, the danger of inflation would be removed, but at the same time the farmers would receive a price equal to the cost of production. They would be able to put these war savings certificates into a sinking fund, so that at the end of the war these certificates could be used to pay off the debts which the farmers are bound to incur as a result of not being able to get the cost of production. If the minister will not answer that, perhaps the Minister of Finance would? Well, we will raise it on the appropriation.

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, ^Vlarch 26, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1943, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Some days ago I asked if the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) would make a statement on air raid precautions on the two coasts, and I believe he is prepared to make that statement.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): A few days ago, and again last evening, I was asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) to make a statement, to which he has just referred, on air raid precautions on the Pacific coast. I think it may be preferable if I discuss the subject as it affects all parts of the dominion that have been designated for organization of A.R.P. work. Then, if necessary, I can particularize with regard to the Pacific coast area.
Air raid precautions basically are those measures which the civilian population can and must take for the protection of their own lives and property. They should not be
confused, as they frequently are, with the defence of the country from attack. That is the function of the armed services. The functions which make up air raid precautions are the ordinary functions of a municipality, such as patrolling the streets, fighting fires, conveying injured persons to hospital, repairing damaged public utilities, demolishing damaged buildings, et cetera. These are functions for which every municipality is normally equipped and organized up to a point, namely, to the extent necessary to cope with normal hazards. It is recognized that enemy air raids or bombardments greatly accentuate the degree of risk, and the ordinary municipal services must be greatly expanded in the interests of the public safety. It is considered that this expansion should take place in two ways, personnel and equipment, neither of which should impose any substantial or unbearable expense upon the municipal exchequer.
In regard to personnel, the number of trained and available personnel can be and has been increased through enrolment, training and organization of volunteers. There is nothing foreign to our genius in this method. In the smaller municipalities fire fighting and many other public services are performed by volunteers. The A.R.P. programme contemplates extension of this method into the larger cities where people have been accustomed in normal times to leave their public services to professionally trained experts.
In regard to equipment, the provision of additional equipment to meet the war emergency has been assumed by the dominion government. Thus the municipality, which must necessarily assume the direction and control of its own people in the matter of air raid precautions, is not called upon to undertake any great expense. Let me now, for the information of the committee, give a concise history of the development of air raid precautions in Canada.
In March, 1938, the departmental committee formed to consider the defence of Canada in case of war recommended to the cabinet that air raid precautions should be under the jurisdiction of the minister and the Department of Pensions and National Health. This was concurred in by the government. The Minister of Pensions and National Health immediately set up, under the chairmanship of the deputy minister, a committee within the department.
Ruling was made by the Department of National Defence that the following areas in Canada should be considered as subject to definite risk of enemy attack: Sydney, Halifax, Saint John, Quebec City, Vancouver, Victoria,
War Appropriation

attack take place when large numbers of people are in the down-town streets, provision of this type is necessary.
(c)	Public Assemblies. Here the minister has power to authorize a senior police officer to prohibit public assemblies. The minister can and will issue such orders to senior police officers upon the advice of his departmental representative on the ground when any special occasion for it arises. Senior police officers have inherent authority to keep public order, and this regulation is to meet any special emergency.
Black-out. Regulation 35 deals with control of lights, sounds and traffic. It is popularly known as the "black-out regulation". The general provision is that the minister of pensions or any person to whom he has delegated authority may issue orders prohibiting or regulating the display of lights, sounds on roads; to designate signals upon which orders shall become operative.
(Note: No such order shall apply with respect to the navy, army and air services, except with the consent of the minister at the head of the indicated service department.)
The minister of pensions has delegated his authority under regulation 35 to the provincial premiers with the exception of Nova Scotia, where it is delegated to the minister of health and Ontario to the attorney general, with authority to redelegate to provincial ministers and officials. The provincial minister thus commissioned may issue orders for the darkening of lights, the suppression of noises, and for the regulation of traffic, either in connection with an actual air raid or in training for such eventuality. It is for the provincial premier to prescribe the signals, to issue orders, and to enforce them. There is authority in regulation 35 for the provincial premiers to redelegate to officials or to municipal authorities within their own areas.
The three defence ministers have conferred upon the senior defence officer in each area their authority to approve such orders in so far as they may affect the services. However, on December 19, 1941, regulation 35 was amended by adding an additional provision that "no lights other than those used for street lighting purposes shall be displayed in any area	specified in	any order made"pursuant to	the	general	authority of	theregulation. The additional amendment also prohibited the display of lights in business premises except during business hours and while staff is present on the premises. There is provision that these regulations may be removed, either temporarily or permanently, by order of	the	minister	of pensions,	concurred in by	the	Minister	of Munitions	and

Supply. Difficulty was experienced at first in administering this regulation, and a conference was called in Ottawa on February 3, in order that a uniform code of regulations for lighting might be drawn up for the whole of Canada, if considered desirable. At this conference were represented provincial governments, transportation companies, retail merchants, and industry generally.
The conclusions of this conference were, briefly, that the new subsection in section 35 should remain and that each province should request the exemptions which they considered advisable for their particular province. These exemptions, with the exception of Quebec, have been completed, signed by the two ministers and issued. Exemptions were also applied for by the federal district and issued. Compensation.
(a)	Insurance for property:	The Minister of Finance on December 24 announced that a scheme of war risk and bombardment insurance is in course of preparation and that its terms shall have application as from the date of this announcement. This means that any damage caused prior to the enactment of the insurance plan will be covered by the scheme as it may ultimately emerge.
(b)	Personal injuries and death: A scheme of compensation comparable with that of workmen's compensation acts has been adopted by the dominion government for air raid precautions workers who may be injured or killed in performance of their duties as a result of enemy action or during a black-out. The scheme covers registered workers in an authorized air raid precautions organization.
Medical care, hospitalization, compensatory allowances for the injured worker and his dependents, and pension for the dependents of an air raid precautions worker who may be killed are included in the scheme. Administration is in the hands of the Canadian pension commission.
Certain classes of air raid precautions workers are entitled to compensation for injuries or death sustained during the training period. These classes of workers are auxiliary firemen and demolition squads, whose training is considered to involve a certain amount of danger to life and limb.
The order in council providing for compensation is P.C. 7147, of September 10, 1941.
The order in council providing for hospitalization and treatment is P.C. 115/9130, of November 22, 1941.
P.C. 7147 originally dealt with only eleven designated areas. The designated areas were greatly enlarged by P.C. 2/9660, of December 10, 1941 when the entire coastal areas were held to be subject to risk of attack.

War Appropriation
I come now to the types of work involved in air raid precautions. They include:
Patrol of city streets to ensure that regulations are obeyed and to detect and report incidents requiring attention.
Regulation of traffic.
Care of casualties.
Firefighting.
Decontamination in case of gas attack.
Demolition of damaged structures.
Repairs to damaged public utility services.
Transportation and communication services to facilitate the foregoing.
Prevention of panic.
Wardens are expected to become acquainted with all individuals in their respective blocks.
Wardens are expected to survey every house and building in their blocks, and to have full particulars regarding the number of persons domiciled therein, their status as to numbers of infants, invalids, et cetera, the availability of exits, and so on.
Organization Policy. The dominion government undertakes through the Department of Pensions and National Health to provide necessary equipment and supplies, training manuals and instructional literature.
The provincial governments have been asked to form air raid precautions committees and to encourage formation of local air raid precautions committees in the designated areas.
The Minister of Pensions and National Health asked the provincial premiers to be chairmen of the provincial committees, and suggested that the mayors of municipalities should be chairmen of local committees.
It was considered by the dominion government that the bulk of the work must be done by private citizens on a voluntary basis, and that organization and direction would be given to a large extent by permanent dominion, provincial and civic officials, selected from appropriate departments.
Committees were preferred to the rigid municipal organization, because it is considered desirable that groups of municipalities should organize their air raid precautions as a single unit, with provision for cooperation in such matters as firefighting.
Key officers in each area for the actual training and administration of air raid precautions must necessarily be chiefs of police, fire chiefs, medical officers of health and municipal engineers.
The duties to be performed by the voluntary organization are very largely an extension of the duties of the regular police officers, firemen, and maintenance crews of the engineering departments.
It was considered advisable, therefore, that voluntary groups should be trained and
directed by the permanent officials responsible for the various specialized types of activity in which volunteer air raid precautions workers are called upon to assist.
Where voluntary organizations exist, and are equipped to discharge valuable functions in connection with air raid precautions, these have been asked to cooperate in order that new organizations need not be set up.
For instance, the Saint John Ambulance Association has done a notable work in training air raid precautions workers in first aid.
The Red Cross society has also organized for the relief of distress which might arise in a raid.
The suggestion has recently been made that a number of firemen from each of the principal cities might, with advantage, be sent to train at special schools which are being set up in the United States for that purpose.
Already the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, at the suggestion of the director of air raid precautions, has sent one or two men to attend schools on transportation problems. It is believed that those to be trained at these special schools will be able to instruct others.
Care of Casualties. The plan is that air wardens shall patrol the streets and report where casualties occur. There should be in every locality, first-aid posts from which qualified first-aid workers can be dispatched with stretchers and other equipment to bring injured persons to hospitals or other centres where care can be given.
Doctors and nurses should be at key positions where they can supplement the efforts of the first-aid assistants.
The most seriously injured should be transported to hospital in vehicles, organized and held available for this duty. Hospitals should have emergency staff and space available to care for casualties thus brought to them.
Local committees should survey buildings in the vicinity of existing hospitals, wherein emergency accommodation can be given. The Department of Pensions and National Health has supplies of beds and bedding to place in such buildings.
It is considered that general hospitals can, on the shortest of notice, make emergency accommodation available by evacuation of a substantial percentage of their normal patients.
In every hospital there are convalescents and other patients who could, with little disadvantage, be cared for at home. By constantly checking their own population, hospital managements should be prepared to evacuate such patients speedily in an emergency. The voluntary transportation com-
War Appropriation

mittees in the air raid precautions organization can be asked to hold themselves in readiness to assist in the process.
The Saint John Ambulance Association from the outset of the war has assisted in training volunteer air raid precautions workers in first aid. The number of air raid precautions workers holding the association's first-aid certificate, on December 15, 1941, was 12,950.
Shelters. It is a function of local air raid precautions committees to survey their areas for premises in which people may take shelter during an air raid. The minister of pensions has authority to order that such premises may be used, and to restrain the owners or occupants from refusing access.
In all the more exposed areas, the necessary staff work for this purpose has been done so that, in an emergency, orders can be issued at the briefest notice.
Equipment. It was considered that the greatest expense would be in connection with the provision of equipment and supplies. This expense the department of pensions has undertaken to meet. Reserve stores of equipment were accumulated before the outbreak of war, and issue was made from these stores to the provinces. The provinces, in turn, were asked to make issue to the local areas.
Municipal areas should requisition their provincial committees for supplies and equipment. The provincial committees will, in turn, requisition the department of pensions.
It is considered desirable that, with respect to many types of equipment, only sufficient for training should be issued to local areas, and the remainder be held in central stores available to meet emergencies wherever they may occur.
The dominion government has, however, allocated small credits to each province for the purposes of financing organization expenses not covered by the provision of supplies and equipment issued from Ottawa. The procedure is for the province or municipality to obtain approval of a proposed expenditure, and then to submit a properly vouched account. The minister of pensions may then authorize payment thereof.
'In Nova Scotia, where a comprehensive system of air raid precautions has existed in the two leading urban areas for more than two years, the original grant of $5,000 for organization purposes has not been exhausted. Supplementary grants were made recently, however, when the areas to be organized were greatly enlarged.
In some provinces, there was a desire on the part of the provincial authorities to broaden the functions of the organization formed for air raid precautions purposes.

In view of the fact that the provincial authorities considered that useful public purposes could be served by asking the air raid precautions organization to assume other duties, the dominion government raised no objection, but it could not undertake financial responsibility for these other duties.
Instructional literature is considered to be included under the heading of "equipment and supplies". Municipalities desiring to issue circulars to all householders have obtained authority to do so, and the Department of Pensions and National Health has paid for the printing and other expenses connected therewith.
The following are the main types of equipment issued:
Badges and arm bands Crutches
Arm and leg splints First-aid haversacks First-aid kitboxes Pouches Stretchers Tarpaulins Anti-gas suits
Rubber boots Protective overalls Berets
Steel helmets Stirrup pumps Iron scoops Fire hose Respirators Fire pumps
Up to the most recent report, equipment had actually been issued to the value of $613,726. Other equipment is on order to the value of $789,642, making a total of $1,403,369. Our estimates for the coming year under the war appropriation bill, aggregate $4,805,000.
The department of pensions has administered air raid precautions up to date very largely by allocating the required duties to members of its regular staff. It is believed that provinces and municipalities can administer in the same way without engaging special paid personnel. This has been done quite successfully in the maritime provinces.
In December, however, when, on the advice of the Department of National Defence, the areas considered subject to risk of attack were very greatly enlarged, it was decided to increase our administrative staff at Ottawa. The Hon. R. J. Manion-a former minister-had offered his services to the government in any capacity in which they could be used. Doctor Manion was good enough to agree to accept the position of director of civil air raid precautions, and at the beginning of the year undertook his duties with his accustomed energy and ability.
The volume of work has been greatly increased by the enlargement of the areas designated for organization, and we now have four officials dealing in a specialized way with subdivisions of the work. Three of these are regular government employees assigned to A.R.P. duties, and the fourth was engaged from outside. It is possible that further additions may have to be made to our A.R.P. staff.

War Appropriation
No direct cash grants to provinces or municipalities have been made, nor can they, with propriety, be made. The dominion government does not delegate even to one of its own ministers the authority to make expenditures of money without prior submission to treasury board and approval of the proposed expenditure in all particulars. It follows that no minister can delegate such authority to a province or a municipality.
In certain areas there has recently arisen a demand for financial aid on a scale quite out of proportion to that accorded to the cities on the Atlantic coast, where efficient A.R.P. organizations have been developed and have operated for two and a half years. In some cities, some of the officials seem to have formed the opinion that effective air raid precautions will require a large paid staff. Our experience with the cities on the Atlantic coast suggests definitely that this is not correct, that the various duties can quite effectively be discharged by the ordinary municipal officials with the cooperation of volunteers. I am not, however, prepared to say that conditions in any two cities are identical and that because local conditions in one city permit a thing to be done, every other city can necessarily achieve the same results in exactly the same way.
Accordingly, after reviewing a budget presented by my home city and containing many items which certainly should not be charged against the federal treasury, it was decided to adopt a standard scale of organization and equipment. This suggested "establishment" was recently forwarded to the provincial committees together with a brief statement of dominion government policy with respect thereto. The model establishment took account of variations in population and variations in the degrees of risk as estimated by the government's military advisers. It indicated with regard to each type of city the minimum number of wardens, the number of auxiliary firefighters, the number of roof watchers, the number of first-aid detachments that would be required in such an area.
The scheme was 'heavily annotated, indicating circumstances under which the model scale of establishment should be larger or smaller. Account was taken of density of population, of the types of construction prevailing in an area, and appropriate comment on the variations indicated by such factors was included. This model establishment is not mandatory. The whole secret of air raid precautions is, in my opinion, to rely upon the special genius of the people in each area to work out their own methods. Our model establishment is intended as a guide to them, and also as a guarantee in this sense, that the
dominion government accepts the responsibility to supply equipment up to the minimum standard laid down in the establishment. We undertake to supply such equipment as and when it may be available.
With this in view, the plan itself contains particulars of the amounts of equipment required for an organization of the proportions indicated. With respect to certain types of equipment, such as identifying badges, there should be one item of personal equipment for each A.R.P. worker. With regard to certain other types, however, we need to provide only certain items. There was recently indicated in Vancouver and Victoria an assumption that every warden should receive a suit of protective clothing. This is, of course, quite incorrect. Protective clothing is required only for certain squads, such as the decontamination crews. We have indicated the appropriate number of workers to be trained and equipped for each such specialized activity, and we are prepared to supply equipment up to that number.
While discussing this subject of equipment, I must inform the committee frankly that we *have not been able to supply all the equipment which, according to our own standards, should be available. This is not due to any unwillingness or lack of forethought. It is due to absolute inability to obtain the materials.
Let me illustrate by steel helmets. We placed orders for these in very large numbers right from the outset of the war. As it happened, however, the armed forces also placed very large orders. The requirements of the pensions department for A.R.P. purposes had to take second place, and I am perfectly certain that there is not one air raid warden in Canada who would expect to be supplied with a steel helmet at the expense of a soldier. The limiting factor is, of course, the steel that goes into the helmet. Steel is a vital commodity for every branch of our armed services. Nevertheless we have from time to time obtained supplies of steel helmets, and just recently we found it possible to obtain quite substantial deliveries. These have been distributed as quickly as received to the most vulnerable areas.
With regard to equipment of which there is any shortage, we have had to adopt the principle that the requirements of the more exposed areas on the two coasts shall receive first priority. This has been explained to the provincial committees in the less exposed provinces, and the situation has been accepted in good part. Indeed, when last December the Pacific coast was considered to be under direct menace, the provincial government of Ontario, without hesitation, offered us the
War Appropriation

use of the entire forest firefighting equipment in northern Ontario, and this equipment was speedily transferred to the threatened zone.
As a British Columbian and as a member of the dominion government, I am glad to have this opportunity of expressing publicly the most cordial appreciation and gratitude to the government of Ontario for this unselfish and patriotic act. Only a few days ago the Ontario government again notified me that, if it were not yet possible to return the equipment, they were prepared to have it remain at the coast until we were able to replace it. I wish to assure the committee that every effort is being made to effect replacement at the earliest possible moment, because we are no more desirous of having the forests of Ontario exposed to any hazard from time to time than we are to incur risk for our own people of British Columbia. My fellow citizens of British Columbia are deeply grateful, as I have said, to Ontario for the splendid spirit of cooperation and support exemplified in this loan.
With respect to equipment generally, we have received every possible assistance from the priorities officers of the Department of Munitions and Supply and where we have not been able to meet the full requirements of certain areas, I can assure the committee that the difficulties are real and not due to any neglect.
At the time we sent out our model establishment we also laid down a general policy with regard to federal assistance which I shall state to the committee definitely.
The dominion government is to provide reasonable, initial, organizational expenses to the provinces.
We are to provide booklets and printed matter, and personal equipment-as such is obtainable by us-to the provinces, who will distribute them to the municipalities. The personal equipment for A.R.P. workers will be provided for numbers up to an established strength, as decided by the federal A.RP. office.
Special equipment, such as medical supplies, auxiliary firefighting apparatus, airraid sirens, and so forth-as such is obtainable by us-will be supplied according to local conditions, in amounts considered adequate by the director of air raid precautions. In the case of air raid sirens we will also pay reasonable costs of installation and maintenance. The above supplies will be sent by us to the provincial A.R.P. committee whose duty it will be to allocate them and distribute them to the municipalities concerned. 
The federal A.R.P. office in Ottawa has set up a model establishment for areas designated as liable to attack.
The federal government will pay 50 per cent of A.R.P. expenses of municipalities situated within the vulnerable areas, but such expenses must be kept within reasonable bounds, in every sense of that term.
No new paid staff should be taken on for A.R.P. work, unless absolutely necessary. No salaries may be charged against the federal government for any extra work performed by the regular and ordinary municipal staff.
The same principle is to apply to the use of public buildings or office space. In other words, where public buildings are available for this work, no charge for rent, heat, janitor service or other expenses shall be made. Municipal budgets must be submitted for examination to the representative of federal A.RP. in the area and through him to the provincial A.R.P. committee, or, if we have no representative in the district, then directly to the provincial A.R.P. committee. The latter, after checking the budgets, will send them to the office of the director at Ottawa. Only when the budget has been agreed to by the office of the director will it be recommended to and considered by the dominion government as one on which the 50 per cent may be paid.
It may strike hon. members as remarkable that, in two and a half years of war, this is the first fairly comprehensive statement with regard to air raid precautions that has been made to this committee. There is a very definite reason for that. As has been stated, we regard air raid precautions as essentially a local activity. The work is done very largely by volunteer workers. A successful scheme requires that every citizen shall have some knowledge of what will be expected of him in the hour of emergency. Therefore our effort at Ottawa has been to encourage the provincial and municipal officials to take the leadership in their own areas. We have felt that the more they rely upon their own efforts, the better the programme will be carried out. Or, to state the opposite, the more the local people are encouraged to look to far-away Ottawa for leadership and guidance at every turn, the less efficient will be their local organization. My policy, therefore, has been to keep quiet in regard to certain controversies that have arisen. We are glad and anxious to help where we can and when we are asked.
Our A.RP. officers have visited the various areas repeatedly to give advice and assistance, especially to help with that type of advice which comes from knowing what is going on in a number of centres. Each city or province has developed out of its own genius especially

War Appropriation
successful measures in some one particular field. Our federal officers are able to pass this information along to others.
We have sought no publicity. We have felt that the spotlight should rest on the local leaders, the chairman of the provincial and municipal committees. In the hour of emergency it is they who will have to take the responsibility and to whom the people must learn to look. There have been numerous misunderstandings and occasional lack of cooperation, but by and large the spirit of cooperation has been excellent. As compared with England, where I had opportunity last year of personally inspecting the wonderful A.R.P. organization, we have been one happy family. Their magnificent system of air raid precautions has been developed out of strife and friction and grief and bitter experience.
Despite all their precautions, when the great fire attack was made on London they were largely caught unawares; yet in a few days they managed to develop a system of defence such that I am confident no incendiary attack can ever again succeed in that great city. We have the benefit of studying their experience under actual fire, and we have maintained continuous contact with their organization, so that we know of their mistakes as well as of their successes. We have been strongly advised to avoid some of their most outstanding methods, methods which they would not adopt if they were starting from scratch again. This advice has been quietly passed along to our provincial and municipal committees, and I believe the responsible heads of the local organizations are reasonably well informed.
Large public shelters, and evacuation of population, are two measures that we believe to have been mistaken, and most of the authorities in Great Britain now agree that that is so.
In conclusion, I wish to pay my tribute to the tens of thousands of voluntary workers for their untiring efforts to build up in their own towns and cities an efficient system of air raid precautions. I wish also to pay my tribute to the provincial and municipal committees, consisting partly of public officials and partly of private citizens, who have given splendid leadership to their communities. In no aspect of our war effort have the people of Canada demonstrated more fully their loyalty and willingness to cooperate for the public welfare. The number of voluntary workers is now in excess of 150,000. All of these people have taken training courses in some phase of A.R.P. work. It is upon them that success depends.
This is an activity in which every man and woman must be prepared to do his or her part.
Old London learned a year and a half ago that the city fire department cannot cope with an incendiary raid. Every man must learn to be his own fireman; every woman in the home must know how to deal with a fire bomb on her own doorstep, or her own rooftop. Others will be too busy to help. Therefore I appeal to the people of this country to take this matter very seriously and that each one learn from the wardens in his own city block what measures he must be prepared to take. This is one phase of war effort that cannot be left to somebody else. It is the responsibility of each and every individual man and woman.
I think I have now gone into the matter fairly extensively and answered the questions asked by the hon. member for Vancouver
East.
Mr. GRAYDON; I should like to ask the minister a question. I know he will not take it as a reflection on his splendid work in connection with the departmental activities which he has just analysed, but last May I asked a question in the house, and the Prime Minister subsequently answered it, as to whether or not the Canadian government had under consideration the matter of appointing a minister of home security, as was done in Great Britain.
I should also be very glad if the minister would outline the reasons, to which I am sure he must have given much consideration, which led to the discarding of the idea that was then advanced.
In addition, I should like to ask as to the blackout method. I know there has been considerable controversy as to the efficiency of the blackout method of defence against air attack. Many people have pointed to the fact that Moscow, one of the great targets, used the direct searchlight method of warding off aerial attacks, while an article in a prominent magazine in Canada a week or so ago stated that there had been some change of opinion among authorities with regard to the efficiency of the blackout method as opposed to the searchlight procedure. Would the minister clarify those two points at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Regarding the first point I do not think my hon. friend would expect me to answer. That is entirely for the Prime Minister, and I shall be glad to direct his attention to the question.
With reference to the blackout method, my hon. friend has correctly stated that it is now a matter of controversy in London. In our entire organization in Canada we have followed the British system. We have the very latest details of the system used in Moscow, and I do not feel confident to

War Appropriation

express a technical opinion as to the merits of the blackout as against the other system. We have had visitors from Britain here; we have been over there ourselves, and in every case we have modeled our organization upon theirs, which by and large stood up pretty well to the attacks made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does the minister believe that it is possible to follow the British system entirely in view of the very different conditions existing in Canada? I hope he has taken that into consideration. No doubt he has.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We shall do that as things develop.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is the policy of the government in regard to the establishment of air raid shelters?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I mentioned that, according to recent advices we have received, the policy is against the adoption of air raid shelters.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I wish to thank the
minister for his exhaustive view of this matter. I do not know about other parts of Canada, but I know the people in British Columbia, and particularly in Vancouver, were much disturbed over this question. There was a very general feeling that air raid precautions, so far as British Columbia was concerned, were in a very bad muddle. I am not saying either that they were or that they were not; I am just mentioning some of the opinions that have been expressed, and I think the minister knows them as well as I do. For myself, I have refrained from giving opinions on this matter, as I have refrained from discussing most military matters and other questions in connection with the war. Whenever I found that I had to criticize the government I did so because of its attitude rather than on the facts of any particular matter.
I was surprised to hear from the minister that the provision of air raid shelters had been discouraged, if I understood him aright, and also that no provision was being made for the evacuation of the civil population in case of a raid or military action. That question is of considerable importance in Vancouver, where we are so hemmed in that there is really only one way out. Again I do not know what the technique should be in that case, but I rather believe that the people would feel safer-whether or not they would be safer-if some provision were made for the evacuation of at least women and children in case of bad raids.
The minister gave the number of air raid workers in the whole of Canada. Could he

give the number of workers in the Vancouver area? I should like to know also the amount of the credit granted to British Columbia, and how that credit was allocated among the various municipalities.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In regard to equipment, I have the figure only for the province, because we issue all equipment to the provincial committee, and the allocation is decided by that committee as among the various municipalities. I can get the other information for my hon. friend; I have it, but not here. For British Columbia the equipment delivered so far is valued at S161,823.30.	The value of the equipment
ordered but not delivered is $235,129.19, making a total of $396,952.49.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: And the value of the equipment for all Canada was something like $630,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is what has been delivered. The equipment, both ordered and delivered, for the whole of Canada amounts to $1,560,000, roughly speaking; I gave that figure a few moments ago. In regard to the number of air raid workers in British Columbia, I do not have that information here by municipalities, though I have it in my office. Roughly speaking in the whole province we have some twenty-one thousand workers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We had some of our own officers go over there at the very outset; and though officially we have not had anyone here under government auspices, from time to time experts have come here from England and have travelled throughout Canada lecturing to our various organizations. As I said a short time ago, however, they have established special schools in the United States, and it has been suggested that we might send a few of our auxiliary firemen down there to take short courses, so they could come back with some training in the newest developments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that the dominion government was assuming full responsibility for the necessary equipment and supplies. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is correct, in this sense. We have assumed complete responsibility for all equipment except such as is normal to the peacetime activities of the municipalities, what you might call standard fire-fighting equipment

War Appropriation
and so on. After consultation with the fire chiefs, the underwriters' associations, and others; after obtaining the best advice we could get from sources in England and the United States, we decided to supply only auxiliary fire-fighting equipment. That is why there has been a certain amount of discussion with regard to fire hose, for example. We only supplied one and a half inch hose, whereas the standard equipment would be a larger size.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Take the case of fire-fighting equipment. The cities and towns are called upon to buy far more equipment than they would otherwise require. Why is it the government will not assume any responsibility for that extra fire-fighting equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well, as I have said, the principle has been laid down and followed that we accept responsibility for such equipment as is rendered necessary by the fact that we are at war; that is in addition to the standard equipment. We do not accept responsibility for the replacement of normal fire-fighting equipment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But they require larger quantities of standard equipment in order to prepare against larger fires caused by raids in which incendiary bombs may be dropped. Surely it is only fair that the dominion should assume responsibility for the increased expenditure brought about by reason of the fact that the municipalities have to buy more of the standard equipment than they would otherwise buy.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We carefully canvassed the whole situation with some of the best experts available, and that was the advice we obtained and the advice we have followed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is not necessarily a matter of the best advice we could get from Great Britain or the United States. We should be able to make up our own minds.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We did; we got advice from Canadians too.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In the first place, deliveries of equipment are entirely conditioned by the speed with which we can obtain them. In the second place, Canada is doing more in this regard for her municipalities than any other country. In the United States, though they have voted $100,000,000 to provide for air raid precautions, not a single cent has been given to any municipality.

speechtext: They 'have been in the war only two or three months. We have been in it three years.
