This is the situation. First, we paid preliminary organizational expenses in Canada. In the second place we provided this equipment and even the technical officers. In the third place, similar methods now followed by some of the public-spirited citizens in Vancouver have been resorted to in different cities for the same purpose.
While I understand the natural apprehension of my fellow citizens of Vancouver, as a matter of fact I can tell my hon. friend that Vancouver has received the best treatment of any city in Canada in regard to A.RP. We are doing everything we can. And I must say in regard to my colleagues that they have been absolutely sympathetic in every way in assisting me to get equipment for the Pacific coast as fast as possible.
I must say about the Atlantic coast that they have been remarkably patient. In Nova Scotia they have been magnificent, because
War Appropriation

until recently, they have themselves entirely shouldered, the whole cost of A.R.P. organization. I believe the first small grant we gave them was one of $5,000, and it was not all expended when we made the second small grant the other day. I was told by Doctor Manion, who came back from Halifax a short time ago, that he was there during a blackout, and he said it was one of the most efficient he had witnessed anywhere.
The whole trouble, if I may say so to my hon. friend, is that under the constitution of Canada, which decides what are provincial and federal responsibilities, you have tripartite control. Where you have divided control you are bound to have a certain amount of dissatisfaction and criticism.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does not the minister think that A.R.P. should be a national responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What would happen to-morrow if we made A.R.P. a national duty? There would be a nationalized fire service and police service in Canada. You would step into all cities and take charge of their police and fire-fighting forces. In other words you would interfere with the jurisdiction of the provinces and municipalities. That is where the danger arises. Frankly at the present time I do not think our municipal authorities want that to happen. The real basis of this -whole situation is cooperation. Give control of the organizations to the municipalities and provinces. We have endeavoured to carry that out. Unfortunately there have been a few difficulties here and there, but these are unavoidable. As long as I -have anything to do with the federal end of the matter we will cooperate with every area as best we can to obtain equipment and do all we can to help them in this very necessary work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The minister referred to the various jurisdictions, municipal, provincial and federal. Surely that can scarcely be an argument, in view of the provision of the British North America Ac-t for dominion jurisdiction where peace, order and good government are concerned.
I was struck by the minister's argument in one or two particulars, but it is still not clear to me. The matter we are discussing is one of the most important branches of our whole defence scheme. How do we differentiate by regarding it as the only one to be placed under the jurisdiction of the municipalities, and the provinces and the dominion, while in respect of every other part of our war effort from beginning to end the dominion government alone, and rightly so, has taken the initiative and coordinated the

whole undertaking? As I said last year, I am not criticizing the minister in this respect because I believe he is working under what is no doubt a worn-out policy, so far as his view of the situation facing Canada to-day is concerned. Until we get. a ministry of home security in Canada, where one minister would be the focal point from which all instructions would emanate, a minister who would have full authority and exercise complete supervision with regard to this important part of our national defence, we are going to have in years to come with respect to our whole A.R.P. set-up the same type of criticism that we have heard during the last few months. It is the most natural thing in the world that the municipalities and provinces should attempt to shift some responsibility from one to the other, but I think the time has come- and I am not speaking only for myself-for the setting up of a ministry such as I have described. There are many people permanently and closely identified with A.R.P. work and civilian defence who have expressed similar views to those I am expressing to-day. I feel keenly on this particular point. Undoubtedly it is most important, and the government should not for one moment remove it from consideration. I repeat that I do not see why we should separate this equally important branch of our national defence from the other branches. Why should we single it out for special attention and divide the supervision in respect to it into three different jurisdictional branches?

He was in charge of that work, in cooperation with the ministry of health.

Who is it in Ottawa who revises the estimated expenditures sent down by cities in connection with this A.R.P. work? A budget was sent down by Vancouver, and it was turned down by some board in Ottawa. Quoting again from a newspaper clipping having reference to the city engineer:
Mr. Brakenridge prophesied that "if things get tougher" the dominion and provincial governments would be forced to take a greater hand in the development of A.R.P.
A.R.P. in Vancouver had accomplished a great deal, but had been consistently hampered by a lack of funds, largely due to refusal of Victoria and Ottawa to approve city expenditures.
The A.R.P. here is really between the devil and the deep blue sea. It has no power to raise money.
When we want something we have to go to Victoria, and our request is then sent to Ottawa. Ottawa generally replies "we don't know anything about this."
This is an impossible condition. I wish the minister would explain just how these matters are handled.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think we should try to
discuss this matter as calmly as possible. Air raid precautions are made necessary because of war conditions. The question arises who is responsible for the condition arising out of military operations. I think it has been decided by experience and general practice that there are certain things that the cities and municipalities must do for themselves, unless the whole municipality is to be put under military law and control. Since air raid precaution work is made necessary by military operations, and since it is not desirable to put the municipalities under military control, the question then arises as to the division of expenses and jurisdiction. I think it is sound policy that the dominion government should provide all essential equipment, because the dominion government has taken to itself all the fields of taxation. The fields still open to the municipality are very limited, and they have great difficulty in getting money for the ordinary essential services. If the government can satisfy the municipality-the city of Vancouver in this instance-that the equipment

provided is sufficient and that the government is paying for it, it is only reasonable that the city should assume certain small essential expenditures on account of the work. As has been said, a great deal of the work is being done on a voluntary basis. I have refrained from criticism in this matter because I do not know enough about it. If I had more information I might be able to decide between the contention of the minister and that of the city. I think the minister has made a very reasonable statement.

The defence of Canada regulations provide that the Minister of National Defence shall give the sanction for removal and specify the class or number of people who may be removed from a certain area after a certain time. The arrangements for the removal are not matters for the Department of National Defence or the dominion government; they are made by the local authorities, and in some cities have been made already. The local authorities decide who are to be moved, make the arrangements for the moving-that is the physical removal-and decide where those who are being removed are to go. The Minister of National Defence is given the

power, which power is delegated to the district officer commanding, to make an order which would give legal effect to the removal. This would enable the removal to be made in case somebody objects to it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I want to address a question to the Minister of National Defence, and one to the Minister of National Defence for Air. A great problem confronts the people of Canada, and they are exercising their minds over it. I wish to direct my question and the few observations I desire to make to the very pertinent problem of recruiting.
Coming as I do from Alberta, which has a favourable record in recruiting as compared with other provinces-and in the observations I am about to make I am not in any way casting reflections on my own province or boosting it unduly-I have a few suggestions to make which may be helpful in this time of peril and crisis. I have been critical in my own mind, although I have not hitherto given expression to it, of some of the recruiting methods and practices followed in obtaining men for the army. There are certain conditions, and certain practices which have been followed, which to my mind are not calculated to draw forth to the country's service the thoughtful and self-respecting young men of Canada to-day.
In the first place I would be critical of the recruiting offices as I have observed them in various places. It does seem to me that when we are asking the young manhood of Canada, the self-respecting, self-starting and selfreliant young men of our country, to offer their lives on the altar of sacrifice, they should at least be approached in a spirit and in a manner becoming free citizens of Canada, and be treated as self-respecting indviduals and not as automatons or people who can be pushed around or as people who can be drummed into doing their duty. It has been my observation that men have come for miles to some of our recruiting centres, and men living in our cities have also found their way to these recruiting centres, but where are these recruiting offices to be found for the most part? In out-of-the-way places, on side streets, and in many cases in second or third-rate buildings, poorly lighted, not well kept, not clean or attractive-and there, perforce, the cream of our manhood are invited to come and offer their lives as a sacrifice for this civilization of which we are so proud. It does seem to me that the best is none too good for men who are willing of their own volition to come forward and offer their lives for their
country, and I do think we might well give very thoughtful consideration to that phase of our war effort so far as the army is concerned.
I am glad to say that in my own home city within very recent months the army have moved the recruiting centre and have now got it in a fine office building centrally located, well lighted, cleanly kept, and where the volunteer is met by a civilian. The results have been remarkable. Why cannot we have decent recruiting offices across Canada, not merely in centrally located buildings but in buildings that are clean and wholesome and attractive, where our men who are volunteers will be courteously received and have no fear of being treated with contempt or be called yellow if they do not forthwith sign up in our forces.
I consider that the young men entering upon an army life, many of whom, in fact the very best we have, come from rural communities, would respond much more readily if they were met by civilians whom they would meet on equal terms, and with whom they could discuss their problems. Many of these young men who come to the cities to volunteer do not know for which particular branch of the service they are best qualified by training, experience and education, and in many instances they are met by an old recruiting sergeant and hustled in, it being taken for granted that they must join the army when they might be much better fitted for one of the other services.
I have also heard complaints and severe criticism of the recruiting centres themselves and of how they are maintained. I know of several men, including myself, who have gone into recruiting centres where there seemed to be no anxiety to meet or welcome you or any great concern whether you were there or not or as to the nature of your business.
Another criticism I have heard is of the treatment of the volunteer in many of the recruiting centres. In my own city of Calgary the recruiting office until recently was on a side street, and after arriving there the recruit was marched a mile and a half or two miles to another place for his medical examination. Then he was marched another mile or two to undergo a dental examination, and finally he would be told: "If you will come back tomorrow we will be able to tell you whether we can use you." Imagine having to go a mile and a half to be examined by a dentist, to find out whether your teeth are satisfactory!
Many of these young men who are coming forward have come miles and miles at their own expense to lay their lives on the altar of sacrifice for their country, only to be told that they will have to wait over until to-morrow
War Appropriation

at their own expense. It does seem to me that that is something which can and should be corrected. These men should be provided with accommodation, and given every consideration and consultation and advice. They should be treated as individuals. It has been my conception that fundamentally what we are fighting for in this war is for the rights of individuals, and it ill behooves us in any of our forces to treat the young men who are coming forward as recruits as other than self-respecting men wishing to do the right thing. We should respect the highest thing about them, their individuality and their personality.
I think that a great deal more inspection and supervision should be given to the recruiting centres as such and to the personnel who examine the men who are offering their lives. Why should the medical man whom I visit in his office as a private individual treat me any differently when I come forward to offer my life for my country? Yet does the young recruit take off his shoes and socks and disrobe in a clean room? Are there the same sanitary conditions as prevail in that doctor's own office were I to consult him in private? Ask any recruit; ask the men in the army to-day, whether those conditions prevail. It is not unknown that volunteers who came forward have, because of the delay and the treatment which they experienced, returned home and never bothered to wait and see what was the result of their examination. I suggest to the government and to the department that such conditions and treatment may be an explanation, at least in part, of the fact that we have not had as many volunteers for the army as, possibly, we should have liked.
I wish, however, to commend the government for the improvements being adopted and the army for the revision of the methods being used so far as the equipment, dress and treatment of the men are concerned. That instead of the battle dress we have given the soldier a walking-out uniform is something of which we should be very proud. One has felt we owed an apology to the boys who have come forward in thousands in past months and had only one uniform in which they worked, a battle dress, thus being compelled to go in these work clothes to their home or to see their sweethearts. You would not do it; your friends would not do it; the ordinary average working man does not do it. Yet these "right honourable" men, the only men who, to my way of thinking, are really entitled to that title, who have offered their lives for their country, have had to go home to greet their loved ones in a working suit-a glorified wind'breaker.
Progress reported.
